question: What are advantages and disadvantages of top methods for picking the right number of topics in topic modeling?

sections.title: The Challenge of Topic Selection
sections.text: Determining the appropriate number of topics is a challenging step in topic modeling [1]. There is likely no single correct number of topics for any corpus, but rather several good options, each of which may be useful [1]. Consequently, the process requires subjective decisionmaking informed by the data and specific research questions [1]. While topic modeling is a good tool for uncovering broad subject-matter-based themes, it is not suitable for subtle nuances, which will still require human coding [1]. Tutorials describe tools researchers can use to identify the number and labels of topics to assist in this process [1].

sections.text: A proposed optimal topic number selection method better selects the appropriate number of topics for the LDA model compared with several other methods [2]. In terms of computational efficiency, the optimal topic number selection method takes less computational time than the perplexity method for the selection of topic numbers for the word-embedding LDA model [2]. High values of congruence indicate high semantic overlap and may be indicative of robust topics, supporting the validity of such multi-faceted approaches [1].

sections.title: Limitations of Common Metrics
sections.text: Commonly used methods include perplexity, JS divergence, and coherence, which were compared on the WOS_46986 dataset [2]. However, the validity of semantic coherence is inconsistent [1]. A specific limitation of semantic coherence is that it is highest when the number of topics is low [1]. Although this metric has corresponded with human judgments of the logical consistency of a topic, its behavior can be misleading [1]. Furthermore, estimating more topics tends to improve fit metrics but diminish coherence [1]. The HDP method, for instance, selects a much larger number of topics than the true number, whereas the proposed method's score curve is closest to a U-shape, finding the optimal extreme [2].

question: The following paper focuses on a problem of counting the number of subgraphs in a graph that have certain properties.  What are the most significant downstream applications that either are or could be using these algorithms?  Concrete examples of the graph algorithms in use in real-world applications would be especially helpful.  https://arxiv.org/pdf/2407.06801

sections.title: Biological and Bioinformatics Applications
sections.text: Subgraph counting serves as a critical tool in the analysis of complex biological systems, with applications spanning biology, bioinformatics, and the study of gene transcription networks [2] [3] [1]. A primary use case involves the detection and counting of subgraphs within protein interaction networks, which enables researchers to investigate molecular pathways and cellular processes across different species [3]. These methods are also applied to the study of neural networks, allowing for the identification of network motifs that characterize biological and computational structures [2]. The search for fast algorithms in this domain is driven by the practical need to process large-scale biological data efficiently, rather than being purely a theoretical pursuit [1].

sections.title: Database Systems and Join Estimation
sections.text: In the domain of database systems, subgraph counting has specific and significant downstream applications, particularly in join selectivity estimation [3]. Sublinear-time algorithms designed for counting star subgraphs are directly applicable to this task, allowing database engines to estimate the size of join results more accurately and efficiently [3]. This capability is crucial for query optimization, where precise selectivity estimates help determine the most efficient execution plan for complex database queries [3].

sections.title: Algorithmic Approaches and Complexity
sections.text: The development of these applications is supported by various algorithmic strategies, including a GraphBLAS approach for subgraph counting and randomized algorithms such as the extensor [7] [8]. The fundamental problem of subgraph counting in large input graphs has a rich history, with recent advances focusing on achieving subquadratic time complexity for graphs with bounded degeneracy [6]. While the exact counting of constant-size subgraphs is polynomial-time solvable, traditional off-line methods that require storing the entire graph are often impractical for large-scale data [5]. Without further assumptions, the best possible algorithm for this problem is likely to have a running time of $f(k) \cdot n^{\Theta(k)}$, highlighting the inherent computational difficulty of the task [4].

question: The Nyquist-Shannon theorem provides an upper bound for the sampling period when designing a Kalman filter. Leaving apart the computational cost, are there any other reasons, e.g., noise-related issues, to set a lower bound for the sampling period? And, if so, is there an optimal value between these bounds?

sections.title: Upper Bound Constraints
sections.text: The Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem establishes a sufficient upper boundary for the sampling period, requiring a minimum sampling frequency of 2.0 Hz, which corresponds to a maximum allowed sampling period of 0.5 s [2]. While rule-of-thumb approaches exist for this limit, the sampling period remains a key index affecting the final estimation error in Kalman filter contexts [1].

snippets: The sampling period is a key index affecting the final estimation error.
hence the minimum required sampling frequency is $2.0~\mathrm{Hz}$ (i.e., a maximum allowed sampling period of 0.5 s) according to the Nyquist-Shannon sampling theorem.
citations.title: stability analysis of networked control in smart grids

sections.title: Noise-Induced Lower Bounds
sections.text: Distinct from computational costs, noise-related issues necessitate a lower bound on the sampling period. Too small sampling periods lead to the deterioration of identification results in the presence of noise, a phenomenon caused by the bias of least squares estimates [4]. A 1985 paper by Sagara, Eguchi, and Wada specifically addressed this by defining the lower bound as the minimum sampling period such that identification accuracy based on step response does not exceed an allowable value [4]. In this framework, initial planning periods can lead to deterioration, and the relationship between the noise-to-signal ratio and the sampling period dictates the limit. Furthermore, as the system order increases, this lower bound becomes larger [4]. Additionally, sampling time should be at least two times less than the minimum system time constant to ensure stability [3].

sections.title: Jitter and Task Model Interactions
sections.text: Scheduling jitters further complicate sampling by deteriorating control performance [5]. When a Kalman filter is embedded in a one-shot task model, it must handle non-uniform samples resulting from these jitters, which produce irregular sampling periods. If samples are corrupted by noise, the operation of the one-shot task model quickly deteriorates [5]. However, experimental results over a noisy plant demonstrate that integrating the Kalman filter with this task model preserves benefits such as noise removal and the elimination of jitter effects [5]. In scenarios involving reference changes, small values are used to appreciate the noisy signal.

sections.text: Despite the existence of both upper and lower bounds, the question of how to select the sampling period properly remains open. There is no single optimal value explicitly defined between these bounds in the provided evidence, as the selection depends on balancing the Nyquist-Shannon limit, system order, noise bias, and jitter characteristics [4].

question: What are different techniques in Non-linear, Non-stationary signal processing? Which one is much effective in view of Geophysical signals?

sections.title: Characteristics of Geophysical Signals
sections.text: The majority of geophysical signals of interest are nonstationary, characterized by the presence of transients, edges, and local oscillations [2]. Specifically, natural seismic P-wave signals are low-frequency in nature, with their energy concentrated in the lower range [1]. Analysis indicates that most of the energy in observed seismic P-waves is concentrated between 0.2 and 1.2 Hz, while the energy in other frequency bands remains relatively uniform and at a low level [1].
